title: Kentucky Common Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: Kentucky common was Louisville's dark everyday beer before Prohibition. Learn its history, recipe and how it tastes.
teaser: A dark, easy-drinking beer from Louisville that nearly disappeared with Prohibition. It is back.
standfirst: Kentucky common was the everyday beer of Louisville for decades before Prohibition closed the city's breweries. It is dark but light-bodied, made with corn and served young. Here is its story and what makes it distinctive.
sections:
In the second half of the nineteenth century, Louisville, Kentucky, was a busy brewing city with a large German immigrant population. Alongside lagers, its saloons poured a local beer that came to be called Kentucky common. Historians believe it was the most widely drunk beer in the city for a long stretch before 1920.

Prohibition, which started in the United States in 1920, ended it. When legal brewing returned in 1933, the style did not come back. It was largely forgotten until historians and homebrewers began digging through old brewing records. The BJCP now lists it among its historical styles.

Kentucky common looks heavier than it is. Its colour runs from amber to light brown, coming from a small amount of caramel or dark malt. Some historical records also mention brewers' caramel. Yet the body is light and the alcohol moderate, roughly 4 to 5.5% ABV in the BJCP guideline.

Bitterness is modest, around 15 to 30 IBU. The flavour is gently malty with a little toast, caramel or light roast and a clean, slightly grainy finish from the corn. Think of it as a darker cousin of cream ale rather than a porter. Our guide to brewing a cream ale at home shows that lighter relative.

Like many American beers of its era, Kentucky common used a significant share of corn, often somewhere around 20 to 30% of the grist. American six-row barley of the time had high protein and plenty of enzymes. Corn diluted that protein, lightened the body and converted easily in the mash. It was also cheap and local.

Kentucky was corn country then and still is. That is also why bourbon developed there. That shared grain gives the region's beers and whiskeys a family connection. Our guide to corn whisky mash bills shows how the same grain behaves in distilling.

For years, many writers described Kentucky common as a sour mash beer, souring the mash the way bourbon distillers sour their mash. Later research into old brewing texts has cast doubt on this. Most historians now think the beer was not deliberately sour. The modern BJCP guideline describes it without sourness.

What the records do show is speed. Kentucky common was fermented quickly, often at ale temperatures. It went out to saloons within days, sometimes still finishing fermentation in the cask. It was a fresh beer, meant to be drunk young, not aged.

That speed shaped its character. With no long cold conditioning, the beer kept a little fruitiness from the ale yeast and a soft, slightly rough edge that a lagered beer would lose. Brewers today who want to recreate it usually ferment around 18 to 20 °C with a clean ale strain, then package within one or two weeks.
Why the style suits a brewpub

A beer that goes from grain to glass in about a week and needs no long lagering is attractive to any brewer short on tank space. Kentucky common uses inexpensive ingredients, ferments fast and offers a talking point that most beer lists lack.

Indian brewers already work with maize as an adjunct in many lagers. Our guide to rice and maize adjuncts in India explains how they are handled. Adding a little dark malt to that familiar base would produce something close to a Kentucky common. It could make a good 4.5% house dark beer for drinkers who find stout too heavy.

Serve it around 8 to 10 °C in a simple pint glass. Look for clarity and an amber to chestnut colour with a modest head. The aroma should be quiet: light caramel, some grain, perhaps a hint of fruity ale yeast.

On the palate it should be dry, light and easy, with gentle malt and just enough bitterness to stop it feeling sweet. Any noticeable sourness probably means infection, unless the brewer has chosen a soured interpretation and says so. Heavy roast or a thick body means the beer has drifted towards porter.

Tasting a revived style like Kentucky common teaches you to judge a beer against its own guideline rather than against what you expect dark beer to be. That is a core skill for any judge or serious taster. It means knowing the style markers and spotting where a beer meets or misses them.

For a first step, taste a Kentucky common alongside a cream ale and a mild porter. Rank them by colour, then by body. You will see that colour and weight are separate things, which is one of the most useful lessons in beer tasting.
faqs: It comes from Louisville, Kentucky, where it was a popular everyday beer before Prohibition began in 1920.
Is Kentucky common a sour beer?
Probably not. Older writing called it a sour mash beer, but later research suggests it was not deliberately soured. The BJCP guideline describes it without sourness.
Usually around 4 to 5.5% ABV, with modest bitterness and a light body.
Why does Kentucky common use corn?
Corn lightened the body, diluted the high protein of American six-row barley and was cheap and plentiful in Kentucky.
